name: Broccoli

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Loam to sandy loam, fertile and well-drained, with plenty of organic matter.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Heavier clay loams are workable if drainage is improved with organic matter; broccoli's shallow roots dislike both waterlogging and drought.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Pure sand drains and dries too fast for a heavy-feeding, moisture-sensitive crop unless heavily amended and watered often.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Broccoli likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but drains well. Mix in compost before planting.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Broccoli performs best in a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter. A consistent, even moisture supply matters for quality heads, so work in compost and avoid soils that either pond water or dry out fast.

ph.note_beginner: Broccoli grows best in slightly acidic to near-neutral soil. A simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a pH near 6.0 to 6.5. Broccoli still does fine across 5.5 to 6.8, and holding the soil at or above roughly 6.8 to 7.0 also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease.

fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 21-0-0, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broccoli is a heavy feeder with a high nitrogen requirement and a small root zone, so place feed near the plant. Use a starter fertilizer at transplanting, side-dress with nitrogen about 3 weeks later, and feed again after cutting the central head to push side shoots. Avoid overdoing nitrogen, which can give soft, poor-quality growth.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Broccoli is hungry and needs steady feeding. Give it a feed when you transplant, again about 3 weeks later, and once more after you cut the main head so it makes side shoots.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your broccoli with nitrogen.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. 21-0-0 side-dress or blood meal. Starter feed at transplant.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a balanced vegetable fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row, then a lighter feed when the head reaches about quarter size.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer.

companions.note_beginner: Broccoli does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce. The main things to keep it away from are other cabbage-family plants, which share its diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most broccoli companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The pairings worth acting on are practical ones: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents, and lettuce or spinach as cool-season intercrops that use space and light before broccoli fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate broccoli from other brassicas, which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill is a classic friend for broccoli. Its strong smell is said to put off cabbage pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for broccoli; their smell is said to help keep cabbage pests away.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young broccoli plants to use the space while the broccoli fills in.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion: aromatic herbs like dill are long held to confuse or deter cabbage pests by scent, and dill's flowers also draw beneficial insects. The effect is a folk-garden one rather than a documented broccoli yield benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest confusion is a well-documented companion tradition for brassicas, but no T1 extension trial documents a dill-broccoli benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional companion for brassicas, their scent thought to deter cabbage pests. It is a classic interplanting practice rather than a T1-tested pairing, and the two share no major pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-deterrence is classic companion lore; no T1 source documents an onion-broccoli benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce is a shallow, quick, cool-season crop that shares broccoli's season and tucks along the bed edge, using space and light while the broccoli is still small. The pairing is space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect, and the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-broccoli benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Spinach
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another quick cool-season green that shares broccoli's window and fits the same space-driven intercrop role along the bed edge. Traditional and low-risk rather than a documented benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season space-use intercrop lore; no T1 source documents a spinach-broccoli benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums are often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but it works best for moderately mobile pests and is not a tested broccoli-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism, but the specific nasturtium-broccoli pairing is not formally tested in T1 trials.

good_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional all-purpose companion said to deter cabbage moths and aphids. The broad pest-deterrent claim is folklore rather than a documented broccoli-specific effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: General pest-deterrent companion lore; no matching T1 pattern for broccoli.

good_seasoned.name: Celery
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing brassica companion said to deter cabbage white butterflies. Traditional lore with no documented broccoli-specific support.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Traditional brassica pairing; no T1 source documents the deterrent effect for broccoli.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep broccoli away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, cauliflower, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts and the other cole crops share broccoli's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. This is a real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the specific bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that broccoli and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tomatoes and broccoli are both heavy feeders and a traditional list pairs them as competitors for nutrients and space. Inter-plant competition is a real general concept, but the specific bad pairing is not documented for broccoli, and the two also want different seasons. Treat it as low-priority caution.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Competition is a real general concept but the specific broccoli-tomato bad pairing is extrapolated, not T1-documented; seasonal mismatch makes overlap uncommon anyway.

pests.name: Cabbageworms and cabbage loopers
pests.symptoms: Ragged holes chewed in leaves and into developing heads, with green caterpillars and dark droppings on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the leaves and head, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
pests.cause: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and heads; the adults are white or brownish moths and butterflies that lay eggs on the leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like broccoli and chew on the leaves and heads.
pests.organic_treatment: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars; hand-pick larvae and eggs from the undersides of leaves. Repeat after rain, since Bt washes off.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and kills only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention: Cover plants with floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults; clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and watch for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover your plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and start watching for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips, leaf undersides, and tucked into the head; leaves curl and pucker, and a sticky residue and sooty mold may appear. Gray-green waxy cabbage aphids are especially hard to wash out of heads.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth, under leaves, and inside the head. Leaves curl up, and there may be a sticky coating. The waxy gray-green kind is hard to wash out of the head.
pests.cause: Several aphid species, notably the waxy cabbage aphid, suck sap from broccoli; they multiply quickly in warm weather and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates heads.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast in warm weather, and their feeding twists the leaves and gets into the heads.
pests.organic_treatment: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the head where aphids hide; repeat every few days.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and inside the head where they hide. Repeat every few days.
pests.prevention: Encourage natural enemies like lady beetles and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not reach the head.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often so they don't reach the head.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy damage stunts or kills seedlings.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt or kill seedlings.
pests.cause: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas; they are most damaging at the seedling stage when a small plant cannot outgrow the feeding.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
pests.prevention: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.cause: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult fly lays eggs at the base of the stem, and the maggots hatch and feed on the roots below.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants. Focus on protecting the remaining transplants from further egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots, you can't really save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon heat, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs instead of normal roots.
diseases.cause: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in the soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell up, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention: Rotate brassicas on a long cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known, since this ties directly to the rotation plan; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow broccoli or its cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools so you don't spread it.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf edges, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease can move into the stem and rot the head.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the edges of the leaves, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread into the stem and rot the head.
diseases.cause: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants to limit spread. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid watering from overhead or touching wet plants.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection can discolor the head.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches show on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. A bad case can mark the head.
diseases.cause: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, keep heads dry, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, keep the heads dry, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, more as heads bulk up.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the head.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and stunted, soft growth; broccoli is prone to root rot in soggy soil.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant looks waterlogged.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, checked growth, and small or bitter heads; any stall in growth hurts quality.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep developing heads dry when you water, since wet heads encourage rot.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to get the head wet when you water.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture through head formation is the most important window for quality.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the head is forming.

start_method.notes_seasoned: For the spring crop, start seeds indoors about 5 to 7 weeks before setting out and transplant roughly 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost; broccoli tolerates light frost. For fall, start transplants in mid to late summer, about 4 to 6 weeks before setting them out as the heat breaks, or direct sow. Set out young, well-rooted transplants with 4 to 6 true leaves, since oversized or cold-shocked transplants are prone to buttoning (tiny premature heads). Harden plants off over 7 to 10 days.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can start broccoli indoors or buy young plants. For a spring crop, start seeds about 5 to 7 weeks before you plant out, and set plants in the garden a couple of weeks before your last frost. For fall, start them in mid to late summer and plant out as the heat eases. Use small, healthy plants, not big leggy ones, and let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; broccoli is prone to root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container broccoli still feeds heavily.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli finishes its cycle in one season and is not overwintered in a pot.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli is grown as a single-season annual and is not held over winter in a container.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Broccoli grows in a pot of at least 5 gallons that is 12 inches or more deep, one plant per pot. Keep it cool, watered, and fed. In warm spots, avoid dark pots and give some afternoon shade.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Broccoli is a large, heavy-feeding plant, so use a container of at least 5 gallons and 12 to 18 inches deep, one plant per pot. Because pots warm and dry quickly, keep moisture even, feed regularly, and in warm regions avoid heat-absorbing dark containers and shade the pot to keep roots cool.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container broccoli needs more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits broccoli well, since it smooths out the steady moisture the crop wants through head formation.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which broccoli likes.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Broccoli is a large, top-heavy plant with a shallow, spreading root system, so choose a wide, sturdy container at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot. A broad, stable base keeps a heavy head from tipping the pot, and the depth and width give the roots room and buffer the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Broccoli grows into a big, top-heavy plant, so use a wide, sturdy pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep, with just one plant per pot. A wide, heavy base keeps the pot from tipping over once the head forms, and the extra room keeps the roots from drying out too fast.

recommended.name: Calabrese
recommended.note: The classic green Italian heading broccoli and the most widely grown type; a dependable open-pollinated choice with a good central head and side shoots.

recommended.name: Green Magic
recommended.note: An early, reliable hybrid with some heat tolerance, which makes it a good pick for the spring-into-warm-weather crop.

recommended.name: Belstar
recommended.note: A widely adapted hybrid that does well in both spring and fall, popular in organic gardens.

recommended.name: De Cicco
recommended.note: An heirloom with a smaller main head but heavy, prolonged side-shoot production, good for a long picking window.

recommended.name: Waltham 29
recommended.note: A cold-hardy heirloom bred for fall and overwintering, with uniform heads that finish in cool weather.

recommended.name: Sun King
recommended.note: A heat-tolerant hybrid that holds up better in warmth, useful at the warm edges of the season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the slot: fast, heat-tolerant types like Green Magic for spring, and longer-cycle, cold-hardy types like Waltham 29 for fall. Side-shooting heirlooms such as De Cicco stretch the harvest, while hybrids give more uniform central heads. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: Green Magic and Belstar are easy, dependable choices. For spring, pick a fast or heat-tolerant variety so it heads before it gets hot; for fall, a hardy one like Waltham 29 works well. De Cicco gives lots of small side shoots over a longer time.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, collards, turnip, radish, kohlrabi), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so brassicas do not follow brassicas for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH at or above about 6.8 also helps suppress it.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant broccoli or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting a few years between them helps avoid soil diseases like clubroot.

bolting.triggers: Summer heat (days at or above about 86°F and nights above about 77°F), oversized or cold-shocked transplants, and prolonged cool spells of 35 to 50°F.
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Time the spring crop to head before summer heat and the fall crop to head as weather cools. Set out young transplants with 4 to 6 true leaves rather than large ones, and choose heat-tolerant, short-cycle varieties for spring.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Grow broccoli in the cool parts of spring and fall so it heads before it gets hot. Use small, healthy plants and pick fast or heat-tolerant varieties for spring.
bolting.note_seasoned: In broccoli, heat-driven bolting (a mature plant rushing to flower) and buttoning (a too-young or cold-stressed plant making a tiny premature head) are distinct problems; both make the crop unusable, and both are managed mainly through timing and transplant size.
bolting.note_beginner: If broccoli gets too hot or too stressed, it flowers early or makes tiny useless heads. Good timing is the main fix.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Broccoli is highly perishable and does not hold at room temperature; warmth quickly yellows the buds and turns the heads tough and strong-flavored. Use it within a day if it must sit out, and refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Don't leave broccoli out at room temperature. It goes yellow and tough fast in the warmth, so put it in the fridge as soon as you can after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; broccoli keeps its quality for roughly 1 week this way. Cold and humidity slow the buds from opening, while washing before storage traps moisture in the head and speeds rot.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store broccoli unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it stays good for about a week. Wait to wash it until you're ready to cook, since washing first makes it spoil faster.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Broccoli freezes well once blanched: cut into florets, blanch about 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that would otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color and texture in storage.
storage.freezer_beginner: Broccoli freezes well if you blanch it first. Cut it into florets, boil them for about 3 minutes, then cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze. The quick boil keeps the broccoli from losing its color and flavor in the freezer.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden and falls off within a few days, so harvest close to when you will use it. The central head and the later side shoots both store the same way; chilling promptly after cutting is the single biggest factor in keeping the buds tight and the flavor mild.
storage.notes_beginner: Broccoli is best right after you pick it and doesn't keep long, so harvest it close to when you'll eat it. The main head and the smaller side shoots that come later store the same way. The most important thing is to get it into the fridge quickly after cutting.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 60 to 75°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves, called seed leaves (the cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and warm. Once you see the first real broccoli leaves (true leaves) after the seed leaves, thin out crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; broccoli is ready to transplant at about 4 to 6 true leaves, roughly 5 to 7 weeks from sowing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. They're ready to move outside when they have about 4 to 6 true leaves, usually 5 to 7 weeks after sowing.
growth_stages.user_action: Harden off seedlings over several days before transplanting; set out young plants rather than oversized ones to avoid buttoning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Before planting outside, harden off the seedlings: set them outdoors for a little longer each day over about a week so they adjust. Plant them while they're still young and small, not overgrown, or they may make tiny premature heads.
growth_stages.log_prompt: How many true leaves does your seedling have?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After transplanting, the plant settles in and builds a leafy frame of large blue-green leaves over several weeks before any head forms.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Once planted out, the broccoli puts on lots of big blue-green leaves for a few weeks. This leafy growth comes before any head appears.
growth_stages.user_action: Side-dress with nitrogen as the plant grows, keep moisture even, and watch for cabbageworms and aphids while the frame fills out.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the plant some nitrogen as it grows and keep it evenly watered. Check the leaves for green caterpillars and aphids during this stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Is your broccoli putting on healthy leafy growth?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?

growth_stages.name: Head forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: A tight central head of immature flower buds appears in the growing tip and enlarges; the buds should stay blue-green and closed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tight head of tiny green flower buds appears in the center of the plant and grows bigger. The buds should stay green and closed.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep water steady and watch closely; once the head is full-sized but still tight, prepare to cut. Heat or stress here causes buttoning, bolting, or loose heads.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily and check the head often. When it's full-sized but the buds are still tight and closed, get ready to cut it. Hot or stressful weather now can make the head loose or cause it to flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Has a central head started to form?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Can you see a head forming in the middle?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: The central head is full-sized with tight, closed buds and no yellow showing; this is the moment to cut, before the buds open into flowers.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The main head is full-sized, the buds are still tight and closed, and there's no yellow. This is the moment to cut it, before the buds open into yellow flowers.
growth_stages.user_action: Cut the central head with about 6 inches of stem while buds are tight; cutting on time triggers side shoots. Harvest in the cool of the morning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the main head with about 6 inches of stem while the buds are still tight. Cutting it on time is what makes the plant grow side shoots next. Harvest in the cool morning if you can.
growth_stages.log_prompt: Did you harvest your central head?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you cut your main head yet?

growth_stages.name: Side shoots
growth_stages.what_to_look_for: After the central head is cut, smaller florets form on side shoots from leaf joints down the stem, especially on side-shoot varieties, continuing for several weeks in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After you cut the main head, smaller broccoli florets grow on side branches lower down the stem. These keep coming for several weeks in cool weather, especially on certain varieties.
growth_stages.user_action: Keep harvesting side shoots while buds are tight to encourage more; keep feeding and watering. Pull the plant when heat or hard frost ends production.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep cutting the side shoots while their buds are tight, which encourages even more. Keep feeding and watering. When it gets too hot or freezes hard, the plant is done and you can pull it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you getting side shoots now?

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest the head before it opens
notifications.title_beginner: Time to cut your broccoli head
notifications.body_seasoned: Your central head should be full-sized and tight now. Cut it while the buds are still blue-green and closed, before any yellow flowers show, to get the best quality and trigger side shoots.
notifications.body_beginner: Your main head should be full-sized and tight by now. Cut it while the buds are still green and closed, before any yellow flowers appear, for the best taste and to get side shoots later.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your broccoli is a heavy feeder. Side-dress with nitrogen now to support leafy growth and head formation, placing the feed near the plant and watering it in.
notifications.body_beginner: Broccoli is a hungry plant. Feed it some nitrogen now to help it grow leaves and form a head. Put the fertilizer near the plant and water it in.

notifications.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your broccoli
notifications.body_seasoned: A hot spell is coming while your broccoli is heading. Heat can cause buttoning, bolting, or loose heads. Keep moisture even, and harvest promptly if heads are near full size.
notifications.body_beginner: Hot weather is on the way while your broccoli is making its head. Heat can make the head loose or cause it to flower early. Keep the soil evenly watered, and cut the head soon if it's nearly full-sized.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Days at or above about 86°F and warm nights during head formation cause buttoning, bolting, and loose heads. Keep moisture even and harvest any near-full heads promptly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot days around 86°F or more, plus warm nights, while the head is forming can make it loose or cause early flowering. Water evenly and cut any nearly-ready heads soon.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Broccoli takes light frost in stride and it can sweeten the heads, but a hard freeze damages exposed heads. Cover plants or harvest mature heads before a hard freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Broccoli handles a light frost fine, and it can even taste sweeter, but a hard freeze can damage the heads. Cover the plants or pick any ready heads before a hard freeze hits.

germination.text_seasoned: Start broccoli seeds indoors at 60 to 75°F; germination is fast, usually 5 to 10 days, and seedlings stretch if light is weak after they emerge.
germination.text_beginner: Start your seeds indoors where it's about 60 to 75°F. They sprout quickly, in 5 to 10 days, and need bright light right away or they'll get leggy.
germination.author: claude_ai

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seed-starting mix; broccoli germinates reliably across a wide soil-temperature range as long as moisture stays even.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp seed-starting mix, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout.
germination.author: claude_ai

seedling.text_seasoned: Transplant at 4 to 6 true leaves, about 5 to 7 weeks old; older, root-bound starts are the classic trigger for buttoning.
seedling.text_beginner: Move seedlings outside when they have 4 to 6 real leaves, around 5 to 7 weeks old. Planting ones that are too old or pot-bound can cause tiny premature heads.
seedling.author: claude_ai

seedling.text_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out, and choose a cool, settled spell rather than the front edge of a warm-up.
seedling.text_beginner: Toughen up your seedlings over about a week before planting them out, and pick a stretch of cool, steady weather rather than just before a hot spell.
seedling.author: claude_ai

established.text_seasoned: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart and side-dress nitrogen as the leafy frame builds; broccoli's shallow roots feed best from nutrients placed near the plant.
established.text_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart, and feed them nitrogen as they grow leaves. Their roots are shallow, so put the food near the plant.
established.author: claude_ai

established.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week through this stage; an early growth check from drought or heat sets up buttoning and loose heads later.
established.text_beginner: Water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, while the plant builds its leaves. Letting it dry out or get stressed now leads to poor heads later.
established.author: claude_ai

head_forming.text_seasoned: Once the head appears, keep water steady and watch daily; heat above about 86°F by day and warm nights during heading cause bolting and loose, open heads.
head_forming.text_beginner: When the head shows up, keep watering steadily and check it every day. Hot days over about 86°F and warm nights now can make the head loose or cause it to flower.
head_forming.author: claude_ai

head_forming.text_seasoned: Keep developing heads dry when you water, since wet heads in cool, humid weather invite rot and downy mildew.
head_forming.text_beginner: Try to keep the head itself dry when you water, because a wet head in cool, damp weather can rot or get downy mildew.
head_forming.author: claude_ai

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut the central head while buds are tight and blue-green with no yellow, taking about 6 inches of stem; harvesting on time is what drives the side-shoot crop.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the main head while the buds are tight and green with no yellow, taking about 6 inches of stem. Cutting on time is what makes the plant grow side shoots next.
harvest.author: claude_ai

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest in the cool of the morning and chill promptly; head quality drops within a few days, so cut close to when you will use it.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the cool morning and get it into the fridge soon. Broccoli's quality drops within a few days, so harvest close to when you'll eat it.
harvest.author: claude_ai

side_shoots.text_seasoned: After the main cut, keep harvesting side shoots while their buds are tight to encourage more; production continues for several weeks in cool weather, especially on De Cicco-type varieties.
side_shoots.text_beginner: After cutting the main head, keep picking the side shoots while their buds are tight, which brings more. They keep coming for weeks in cool weather, especially on certain varieties like De Cicco.
side_shoots.author: claude_ai

side_shoots.text_seasoned: Keep feeding and watering through the side-shoot run; pull the plant once summer heat or a hard freeze ends production and quality falls off.
side_shoots.text_beginner: Keep feeding and watering while the side shoots keep coming. Once it gets too hot or freezes hard and the shoots stop, the plant is done and you can pull it.
side_shoots.author: claude_ai

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Expect one central head of roughly 4 to 8 inches across per plant, followed by a steady run of smaller side shoots over several weeks once the main head is cut. Total yield depends heavily on variety and on whether the weather stays cool enough to keep the side shoots coming.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one main head about 4 to 8 inches wide, and then a few weeks of smaller side shoots after you cut that main head. How much you get depends a lot on the variety and on the weather staying cool.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: The central head matures across a week or two as it reaches full size, and that is the single largest harvest. Side-shoot production then peaks in the cool weeks after the main cut, especially on side-shoot-heavy varieties like De Cicco and Calabrese, and tails off as heat or hard frost arrives.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: The big harvest is the main head, which fills out over a week or two. After you cut it, the side shoots come on strongest in the following cool weeks, then slow down once it gets hot or freezes. Some varieties, like De Cicco, are bred to make lots of side shoots.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cutting the central head while the buds are still tight is what triggers the side shoots, so a timely first harvest actually increases total yield. New growers often wait too long and let the head loosen or flower, which both ends the side-shoot run early and gives a coarser main head.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here's the key thing: cutting the main head while its buds are still tight is what makes the plant produce side shoots, so harvesting on time gives you more overall. It's easy to wait too long and let the head bloom, which makes it less tasty and cuts the side-shoot harvest short.
factors_seasoned: Variety: side-shoot-heavy types (De Cicco, Calabrese) keep producing after the main cut; some hybrids put nearly everything into one large central head and give few shoots.
Temperature: cool weather through heading and the side-shoot period sustains yield; heat triggers buttoning, bolting, and loose heads.
Harvest timing: cutting the central head while buds are tight drives side-shoot production; a late cut ends it early.
Nitrogen and even moisture: this heavy feeder needs steady nitrogen and consistent water to size both the central head and the side shoots.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing broccoli planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Buttoning (tiny premature heads)
failure_diagnostics.cause: Heat, transplant stress, or setting out oversized or root-bound starts.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Hot weather, stress at transplanting, or planting seedlings that were too big or stuck in their pots too long.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: You got a tiny, button-sized head on a small plant instead of a full one. This happens when broccoli is stressed early, often from heat or from transplants that were too old or root-bound when set out, and the plant heads prematurely before building a leafy frame. It is easy to blame poor seed, but the usual cause is a checked start. Next time set out young, vigorous transplants with 4 to 6 true leaves into cool conditions and keep them growing steadily without a stall.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You got a tiny, button-sized head on a small plant instead of a full one. This happens when young broccoli gets stressed, usually from heat or from planting seedlings that were too old or pot-bound, so it rushes to make a head before it grows big enough. It's tempting to think the seed was bad, but a stressful start is almost always the reason. Next time, plant young, healthy seedlings with 4 to 6 real leaves into cool weather and keep them growing without any setback.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Set out young transplants (4 to 6 true leaves) into cool weather and avoid any growth check from heat, drought, or being root-bound.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant young seedlings (4 to 6 real leaves) into cool weather, and don't let them get stressed by heat, dryness, or sitting too long in their pots.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flowering before a head)
failure_diagnostics.cause: Summer heat and long days driving the plant to flower.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Hot weather and long summer days pushing the plant to make flowers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: The plant shot up a flower stalk with yellow blooms instead of forming a tight head. Broccoli bolts when heat and long days signal it to flower, racing past the head stage; once it bolts the head cannot re-form. Growers often plant too late in spring and get caught by early heat. Next time time the crop so heading lands in cool weather, choose heat-tolerant short-cycle varieties for spring, and plant a fall crop that heads as the weather cools.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant shot up a tall stalk with yellow flowers instead of making a tight head. Broccoli bolts (flowers early) when heat and long days tell it to bloom, and once that happens the head won't form. A common mistake is planting too late in spring so the heat catches it. Next time, plan so the head forms in cool weather, use fast heat-tolerant varieties in spring, and grow a fall crop that heads as it cools down.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Time spring and fall crops so heads form in cool weather; use fast, heat-tolerant varieties for spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plan your spring and fall crops so the heads form while it's cool, and pick fast, heat-tolerant varieties for spring.

failure_diagnostics.label: No head or loose, open head
failure_diagnostics.cause: Heat during heading, or a nitrogen imbalance.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Heat while the head is forming, or too much or too little nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: The plant grew lots of leaves but made only a loose, open head or none at all. This usually comes from heat during head formation or from a nitrogen imbalance: too little starves the head, while a late flush of too much pushes leafy growth over heading. People often keep waiting for a loose head to tighten, but it will not. Next time keep nitrogen steady and even, ensure consistent moisture, and time the crop so heading happens in reliably cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant made plenty of leaves but only a loose, open head, or no head at all. This usually comes from heat while the head is forming, or from a nitrogen problem: too little and the head can't fill, too much late on and the plant just grows leaves. People often wait for a loose head to tighten up, but it won't. Next time, feed nitrogen steadily, water evenly, and time the crop so the head forms in dependably cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Keep nitrogen and moisture steady, and time heading for cool weather rather than the edge of summer heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Feed and water evenly, and aim for the head to form in cool weather, not right as summer heat arrives.

failure_diagnostics.label: Hollow stem
failure_diagnostics.cause: Boron deficiency or very fast growth from excess nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A lack of the nutrient boron, or very fast growth from too much nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened: You cut the head and found a hollow, sometimes browned cavity in the stem. This is usually caused by boron deficiency or by growth so rapid (often from heavy nitrogen) that the stem tissue cannot keep up and splits internally. The head is often still edible, so it is more a quality issue than a loss. Next time avoid overfeeding nitrogen, keep growth steady rather than pushed, and correct a confirmed boron shortage with a soil amendment based on a soil test.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You cut the head and found a hollow, sometimes brown space inside the stem. This usually comes from a shortage of the nutrient boron, or from the plant growing so fast (often from too much nitrogen) that the stem can't keep up and splits inside. The head is usually still fine to eat, so it's more about quality than losing the crop. Next time, don't overfeed nitrogen, keep growth steady, and only add boron if a soil test shows you need it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip: Avoid pushing growth with excess nitrogen; correct a confirmed boron deficiency based on a soil test.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Don't push fast growth with too much nitrogen, and only add boron if a soil test says it's low.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Broccoli crops in the cool shoulders of the year, so plant in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks within the spring window and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. The spring window is short because heads must size up before summer heat arrives, so most gardens fit only a sowing or two before the midsummer gap; the fall planting, heading into cooling weather, is often the more reliable crop.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant broccoli in spring and again in late summer for fall, in small batches a couple of weeks apart, instead of all at one time. Skip the hottest part of summer, since broccoli will not form good heads in the heat.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up north, grow broccoli twice a year in the cooler weather at each end of the season. Plant your spring crop a couple of weeks before your last frost date so it makes heads before summer heat, and harvest starting in early summer. Then plant a second crop in mid-July for a fall harvest. The fall crop often tastes better and lasts longer because broccoli likes cool weather, and in the milder cold zones it can give you more than the spring crop. Pick fast-maturing varieties in the coldest areas, and keep a row cover handy to protect young plants from a late spring frost or an early fall one.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold zones broccoli runs as two frost-bracketed crops. Set spring transplants out about 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost (roughly late April into May in zone 3) so heads form during the cool, lengthening days before summer heat arrives, then harvest from late June. A second crop goes out in mid-July, timed to head as nights cool in September and October; fall broccoli often eats sweeter and holds longer in the field because cool weather suits it, and in zone 6 to 7 it frequently out-yields the spring sowing. Midsummer is the gap, not a heat exclusion you plant around: nights stay short enough that the limit on both ends is frost, not the day-and-night heat that stalls heading farther south. Lean on fast, short-cycle varieties in the coldest zones, and use row cover at both shoulders to buffer late and early frosts.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf Coast, broccoli is a fall, winter, and spring crop, not a summer one. Plant transplants in mid-January once hard frosts are past, and again in early fall as the heat eases, for harvests that can run from spring all the way to December. Summer is too hot: from about June through August, the heat keeps broccoli from making a proper head, so skip planting then. Aim to have heads forming in cool weather, and choose heat-tolerant, quick varieties for the warmer edges of the season.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Along the Gulf and coastal plain broccoli is a cool-season crop grown right through the mild winter, not in summer. Set transplants out from mid-January as frost danger passes (zone 8) and again as summer heat subsides in early fall, and you can keep a harvest running from spring into December. The hard limit here is summer: from about June through August, days at or above roughly 86°F and nights above 77°F stop broccoli from forming a tight head, so those months are a planting gap rather than a window. Time both the spring finish and the fall start so heading lands in genuinely cool weather, and favor heat-tolerant, fast varieties for the shoulders where the season bumps up against that summer heat.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, grow broccoli from fall through spring, around the cold of winter. Set out transplants any time from December through February; the plants make heads in cool weather and you harvest from late winter into spring. Summer is too hot for heading, so don't plant from about June into early fall. The coldest weeks of winter slow the plants down but won't kill them. Time your planting so the heads form and you harvest before summer heat sets in.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the interior valleys broccoli is a fall-through-spring crop that brackets the cold of winter at both ends. Transplants go out across a long window from about December through February, heads form in the cool, short days, and harvest can run from late winter into spring. Summer is the exclusion: valley heat well above 86°F by day stalls heading, so the months from roughly June into early fall are a no-plant gap, and the coldest midwinter weeks pause growth without killing the crop. Plan plantings so heads finish before that summer heat, and on the cool-winter end use the mild spells to keep a steady succession moving.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along California's cool, foggy north coast, broccoli has one of its longest growing seasons. Plant transplants from February onward and you can harvest from spring into early winter. There's a short cold slowdown in midwinter in the cooler spots, but the mildest coastal areas grow broccoli almost all year. Summers near the coast usually stay cool enough that the heat doesn't stop heads from forming. Plant a little at a time through the mild months for a steady supply, and keep an eye out for downy mildew in the damp coastal air.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, marine-influenced north coast gives broccoli one of its longest seasons, but the window is not quite continuous. Transplants set out from February into spring head through the long mild stretch, and harvest can carry from spring into early winter. A short midwinter cold pause checks growth in the cooler interior pockets (zone 9), while the mildest coastal sites (zone 10) run nearly year-round. The fog belt keeps summer temperatures off the heading-stall threshold most years, so the practical limits are the cool winter shoulder rather than summer heat. Keep an even succession through the mild months and watch for downy mildew in the damp, cool air.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's south coast, broccoli grows through the mild winter and the cooler months around it. Plant transplants starting in January and harvest into late October. Summer is the problem here, not winter: from about June on, it gets too warm for broccoli to form good heads, so don't plant for a summer harvest. Winters are mild with little frost, so the main job is finishing the crop before summer heat. Pick heat-tolerant varieties if you're planting toward the warmer end of the season.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the south coast broccoli is a cool-season crop grown across the long mild winter and shoulders. Transplants go out from about January, heads form through the cool months, and harvest runs into late October. The limit is summer heat: from roughly June onward, warm days push past the heading-stall threshold, so summer is a planting gap rather than a window. The mild winters mean little to no killing frost, so timing is about ending the crop before summer rather than protecting it from cold. Favor heat-tolerant varieties for plantings that push toward the warm shoulders.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, grow broccoli as one winter crop planted in fall. Set out transplants in September once the extreme heat eases, and harvest from about November into February. Summer is far too hot for broccoli, so there's just the one fall planting, with no spring crop. Get your plants going before the short, cool days of midwinter slow them down, and water steadily, because the dry desert air dries out the soil quickly.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the desert valleys broccoli is a single fall-planted winter crop, the inverse of the cold-zone pattern. Transplants go out in September as the worst heat breaks, heads form through the warm fall and mild winter, and harvest runs from about November into February. Summer is simply off the table: desert heat is far too high for heading, so the season ends rather than pauses, and there is no spring planting to add. Get plants established before the short days of deep winter slow growth, and keep moisture even, since desert air dries containers and beds fast.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry areas of southern New Mexico and West Texas, grow broccoli in spring and again in fall, around the hot summer. Plant your spring crop from mid-February to late March, a couple of weeks before the last frost, so heads form before it gets hot. Plant a fall crop in mid-July for a harvest as the weather cools. Summer in between is too hot for good heads. Water evenly in the dry air and sun, and use fast, heat-tolerant varieties for the spring crop, which has the shorter window.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas broccoli runs as a spring and fall crop around the summer heat. Set spring transplants out from about mid-February to late March, a couple of weeks before the last frost, so heads form before the heat builds, then plant a fall crop in mid-July to head as the weather cools. Summer in between is too hot for reliable heading, and the coldest winter weeks pause growth without ending the crop. The dry air and intense sun make even moisture and timing the whole game; favor short-cycle, heat-tolerant varieties for the spring crop, which has the narrower window.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, broccoli is one long winter crop. Plant transplants any time from about August through mid-February; they make heads through the mild winter and you harvest from October into April. Summer is far too hot, so there's no second planting. Plants set out in early fall may need a little shade and steady water to handle the leftover heat while they get established. The long planting window lets you plant a bit at a time to spread out the harvest.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the low desert of Arizona broccoli is a single long winter crop. Transplants go out across a wide fall-to-winter window from about August to mid-February, heads form through the mild winter, and harvest can run from October into April. Summer is entirely out, so there is no second planting; the whole crop sits in the cool half of the year. Early-fall plantings must push through lingering heat to establish, so shade and steady water help young transplants, and the long window lets a succession spread the harvest across the winter.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula, broccoli grows through the mild winter. Summer is too hot and humid for broccoli, so there's no summer planting, just the cool season. Plants set out early in fall deal with leftover heat and afternoon storms, so choose heat-tolerant varieties and try to keep the heads dry when you water to prevent rot.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula broccoli is a cool-season crop grown across the mild winter. Transplants go out over a long fall-to-winter window from about mid-September to mid-February, heads form in the cool months, and harvest runs from November into April. The peninsula's summer heat and humidity end the crop rather than pause it, so the season is the cool half of the year with no summer planting. Early plantings contend with lingering heat and afternoon storms, so favor heat-tolerant varieties for the fall start and keep developing heads dry to limit rot.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, grow broccoli in the cooler months rather than all year round, especially at lower elevations. Plant transplants from about November into December, and harvest from January into March, the coolest part of the year. It rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold: the steady warmth at low elevation can keep broccoli from forming a tight head, so plant in the cool season and choose heat-tolerant varieties. Up at higher, cooler elevations the season runs longer.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii broccoli is grown at the cooler, higher-elevation end of the year rather than as a true year-round crop. In the lowlands the practical window is the cooler months: transplants go out from about November into December, heads form through the coolest part of the year, and harvest runs from January into March. Persistent warmth at low elevation pushes against tight heading, so timing the crop into the cool season and choosing heat-tolerant varieties matters more here than frost, which is essentially absent. At higher elevations the cool season stretches longer, but the lowland default is this bounded winter window.

description_seasoned: Broccoli is a cool-season brassica grown for its tight head of immature flower buds, harvested before the buds open. It performs best in the cool shoulders of spring and fall, bolts or fails to head in summer heat, and rewards a steady supply of moisture and nitrogen. After the central head is cut, most types keep producing smaller side shoots.
description_beginner: Broccoli is a cool-weather vegetable grown for its green head, which is really a cluster of flower buds you pick before they open. It grows best in spring and fall, not summer heat, and keeps making smaller side shoots after you cut the main head.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut the central head while the buds are tight, blue-green, and still closed, before any yellow flowers show, taking about 6 inches of stem. Side shoots then form for later picking.
harvest_ready_beginner: Cut the main head while it is firm, green, and tight, before the little buds open into yellow flowers. More small shoots grow afterward.
soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained bed before planting and confirm pH is around 6.0 to 6.5. Broccoli feeds heavily and roots shallowly, so a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil pays off.
soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into loose, well-drained soil. Broccoli is a hungry plant and likes rich ground.
